results.title: Lead Poisoning in Raptors
results.text:
Lead poisoning is the reserve's most preventable raptor health problem. Birds ingest lead from spent ammunition in carcasses and from fishing weights. Even small amounts can cause weakness, blindness, digestive problems, and death.

The reserve banned lead ammunition in 2019. Visitors, staff, and researchers must use non-lead shot or slugs. The ban is written into the charter and the research permit.

In October 2024, the reserve treated an adult female peregrine named Juniper. Her blood lead level was 0.42 ppm, well above the 0.2 ppm threshold. She was treated for 18 days and released. The case cost USD 6,200 and is documented in rr-037.

The 2025 sampling program tested 12 raptors. One bird was above 0.2 ppm, or 8.3 percent of the sample. The management plan target is below 10 percent, so the reserve is inside the target but not by much.

Staff should report any bird that is lethargic, unable to stand, or has drooping wings. Do not handle the bird without gloves. Call the veterinarian and keep the bird warm and quiet.

## Why this matters

Lead Poisoning in Raptors connects the bird survey to the habitat and the food web. A change in one species is hard to interpret without the prey base, the weather, and the nesting sites. The reserve tracks all of them together.

## How the reserve measures it

The field team uses the standard protocols: six count stations, three nest visits, 60 live traps, and the 20-camera network. Observations are entered within 24 hours. The ecologist checks the records before the weekly summary and the annual report.

## What the data shows

The 2025 season was a high vole year, which improved the outlook for harriers and short-eared owls. The 2024 season was average. The reserve treats a single year as a signal, not a trend, and waits for at least three years before changing a management target.

## Seasonal timing

results.title: Breeding Season Report 2024
results.text:
The 2024 breeding season monitored 44 raptor territories. Of those, 35 were occupied, 26 were successful, and 57 chicks fledged. Overall fledging success was 74 percent.

The season was difficult. A late May storm destroyed two osprey nests and one red-tailed hawk nest. A red-tailed hawk chick was found with a wing fracture and was treated by the veterinarian. The adult female peregrine, Juniper, was found with lead poisoning on 9 October 2024 and was released after 18 days of treatment.

The species totals were: osprey 14 pairs and 19 fledged; red-tailed hawk 9 pairs and 11 fledged; northern harrier 6 pairs and 7 fledged; American kestrel 4 pairs and 7 fledged; short-eared owl 4 pairs and 4 fledged; barred owl 3 pairs and 3 fledged; peregrine falcon 2 pairs and 2 fledged; merlin 1 pair and 2 fledged; bald eagle 1 pair and 2 fledged.

The 2025 season improved because the vole population increased and the spring weather was calmer. The reserve cautions that two years are not a trend. The 10-year occupancy analysis (rr-045) is the better guide.

The full nest table and the disturbance log are in the annual data release.

## Background

Breeding Season Report 2024 is part of the reserve's long-term monitoring program. The question is whether the island's raptor population is changing, and whether the change is driven by weather, prey, disease, or human disturbance. The reserve has collected comparable data since 2016.

## Methods

The analysis uses the standard field protocols. Counts use six fixed stations and a four-hour window. Nest checks use three visits and a 150 m observation distance. Occupancy models use the 2016-2025 records and account for detection probability. The data manager checks the records before analysis.

## Results

The headline numbers are in the document. The full tables are in the annual data release. Estimates are reported with 95 percent confidence intervals. A difference is treated as meaningful only when the intervals do not overlap and the field effort was similar.

## What changed since the last report

results.title: Lead Poisoning Case: Juniper
results.text:
On 2024-10-09, a visitor found an adult female peregrine on the ground near North Point. The bird was weak, had drooping wings, and could not stand. The ranger team captured her with a net and brought her to the clinic.

The bird was known as Juniper, the female of the North Point pair. Her blood lead level was 0.42 ppm. The threshold for clinical concern is 0.2 ppm. She was started on chelation therapy, fluids, and a high-energy diet.

Juniper improved slowly. She gained weight in the first week, began standing in the second week, and was flying in the flight pen by day 14. She was treated for 18 days and released on 27 October 2024.

The total cost was USD 6,200. The source of the lead was never confirmed, but a spent rifle bullet was found in a deer carcass 1.8 km from the territory. The reserve banned lead ammunition in 2019, but the ban does not cover neighboring land.

The case is used in the lead monitoring program and in the visitor center exhibit.

## Purpose and scope

Lead Poisoning Case: Juniper is the standard procedure for this part of the field program. It applies to staff, seasonal employees, and trained volunteers. It does not replace the safety plan (rr-005) or the emergency response plan (rr-006).

## Roles

The head ranger, Elin Ward, owns the procedure. The field lead assigns teams and checks the weather. The data manager, Samir Haddad, checks the records. The veterinarian, Dr. Priya Nair, is consulted for any wildlife handling.

## Procedure

1. Check the weather, the tide, and the radio.
2. Sign out at the research station and record the team.
3. Follow the route and the timing in the document.
4. Record the data in the field form before leaving the site.
5. Report any safety issue, injury, or unusual wildlife behavior to the head ranger.
6. Sign in at the end of the shift.

## Data and records

Records go into the field database within 24 hours. Each record needs date, time, observer, location, weather, and a confidence note. Photos are optional and should not include people without consent. The data manager checks the records before the weekly summary.
